query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings is primarily due to the presence of chemically and structurally complex interlayer interfaces that act as barriers to dislocation motion and atomic diffusion. These interfaces increase the effective stress exponent and activation energy for creep, thereby suppressing rate-dependent plasticity compared to homogeneous (single‐layer) coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: Multilayer coatings composed of high-entropy alloys where each layer is chemically complex and the interfaces are relatively sharp and coherent.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of coatings: one set with a multilayer architecture (with alternating, compositionally distinct high-entropy alloy layers) and a control set with a monolithic, single-layer high-entropy alloy of the same overall composition and thickness.
generation.conditions: High-temperature creep conditions (e.g., 500–800 °C) under constant stress (using nanoindentation or micro-pillar compression tests), where time-dependent plastic deformation (creep) is significant.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemically disordered, compositionally mismatched interlayer regions that introduce local misfit strains and defect structures, which hinder both dislocation glide/climb and atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Under applied stress and elevated temperature, these interfaces impede the motion of dislocations and slow down diffusion-controlled processes by creating localized stress fields and barriers, leading to a higher stress exponent in the creep rate equation and an increased apparent activation energy when compared to monolithic coatings.
generation.predicted_outcome: The multilayer coatings will exhibit a significantly lower steady-state creep rate and a higher stress exponent (n) relative to the single-layer coatings under identical test conditions. A controlled shift in the dominant creep mechanism from diffusion-controlled to dislocation-mediated deformation at higher stresses is expected in the multilayered system.
generation.baseline: Single-layer high-entropy alloy coatings with comparable overall composition and thickness but lacking structured interfaces between layers.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should be observable under high-temperature (>500 °C) and stress conditions where creep is active, and for multilayer architectures with individual layer thicknesses below a critical value (e.g., ~200 nm) to ensure that the interfacial barrier effect is effective. The hypothesis is limited to coatings with coherently bonded layers; strong interlayer delamination or excessive interdiffusion may diminish the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of the interlayer thickness, chemical contrast between layers, and interface quality on the creep resistance is not fully established. Variations in processing conditions that affect interface integrity may also influence the observed behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of coatings – one with a designed multilayer architecture (alternating high-entropy alloy layers with controlled thickness and interface quality) and one as a homogeneous, single-layer coating with the same overall composition and thickness. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature creep experiments (e.g., via nanoindentation under static loads) across a range of stresses.
measurements: Extracted stress exponent (n) from log(strain rate) versus log(stress) plots
Activation energy via temperature-dependent creep tests
Microstructure and dislocation density across interfaces using TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate, an increase in stress exponent, or higher apparent activation energy relative to the single-layer control under the same testing conditions, then the proposed interfacial barrier mechanism as the source of enhanced creep resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Among HEN systems, Al-Cr-Nb-Si-Ti-N quinary coatings demonstrate outstanding potential owing to synergistic strengthening from refractory elements (Nb, Ti) and oxidation-resistant constituents (Al, Cr) [,]. However, there is a lack of research on its high-temperature resistance, oxidation behavior, and corrosion resistance. In this study, AlCrNbSiTiN HEN coatings were synthesized by AIP under controlled bias voltages. The microstructure of the coatings is regulated by controlling the bias voltages to enhance their mechanical properties and high-temperature resistance. The main objective was to fabricate hard coatings that could exhibit favorable oxidation and corrosion resistance and could be used at elevated temperatures. The interaction among bias voltages, coating densification, mechanical properties, and high-temperature stability was systematically studied. The principle of the high-temperature stability of the coatings and their thermal hardness was revealed. Each temperature-dependent curve in the plot can be divided into two distinct regions. Each temperature-dependent curve can be divided into two distinct stress regimes. In the low-stress regime, the extracted stress exponents fall within the diffusion-controlled range defined by Equation (4), whereas at higher stresses, the stress exponent increases markedly, indicating a transition to dislocation-dominated creep. These findings are consistent with atomic-scale observations and corroborate the proposed creep mechanism transitions. Similarly, Figure 9b shows the stress exponent n for HEA, ranging from 1.08 to 11.37. A similar stress-dependent behavior is observed for HEA, with stress exponents evolving from the diffusion-dominated regime at low stresses to dislocation-controlled deformation at higher stresses, following the same mechanistic framework as HESA. Therefore, stress-dependent creep mechanisms in HEA are essentially analogous to those observed in HESA.
